source: De Sabbata et al. (2024/2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: Reward = task reward minus a cost on tokens (value of computation form), trained by Expert Iteration. Model learns to reason less at similar accuracy.
numbers: Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B base, 4 datasets, 1024 train items each. Avg over datasets, 8B: RaM 63.5% acc, 146.2 output tokens; STaR 61.9%, 215.1; CoT few-shot 56.4%, 253.6; Direct few-shot 45.8%, 0 output tokens. 3B: RaM 50.1%/170.8 vs STaR 47.4%/222.7 vs CoT few-shot 34.8%/261.9. Abstract v3: 23-42% fewer tokens.
limits: Only two small base models. Cost weight 0.1 fixed. Needs fine-tuning, not a prompt. Accuracy rescaled, not raw.
agent_relevance: The VOC form (benefit minus cost) works as a training signal. An S0 gate is the inference-time analogue, but we cannot fine-tune.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2024/2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (adaptivity test)
finding: Does it adapt, or just reason less? Split test items by whether direct answering was right (easy) or wrong (hard). RaM widens the length gap between hard and easy.
numbers: Chain length hard vs easy (tokens): 3B-line RaM 145 vs 72 (50.3% shorter on easy); STaR 195 vs 128 (34.4%); CoT few-shot 210 vs 170 (19.0%). 8B-line RaM 139 vs 89 (36.0%); STaR 202 vs 129.5 (35.9%), so no extra gain over STaR there. Instruct models: 0.5-0.9% (no adaptation). Row-to-model mapping read from a garbled table.
limits: The easy label comes from direct few-shot success, a noisy proxy. Instruction-tuned models did not adapt length to difficulty.
agent_relevance: Evidence that heavily RL-tuned models do not size effort to difficulty by default. A scaffold gate must do it.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2024/2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (out of distribution)
finding: Length cut transfers to MMLU-CF but the accuracy gain does not always.
numbers: MMLU-CF: one model RaM 29.5% vs STaR 27.0%, 96.3 vs 150.6 output tokens; the other RaM 36.4% vs STaR 40.2% (-3.8 points, CIs about +-2.4), 110.6 vs 153.6 tokens. Reduction 28-36% tokens. Smaller cut for physics and engineering, larger for fact recall.
limits: One of two models lost accuracy out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Cheap-mode default is safer on recall tasks, riskier on multi-step ones. Fits an S0 gate by task class.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own runs: CoT gain is concentrated in math and symbolic tasks.
numbers: Own evals: 20 datasets, 14 models. On MMLU and MMLU-Pro, up to 95% of the total CoT gain is on questions with an equals sign in the question or output. No features found to predict benefit on non-math questions.
quote: CoT can be applied selectively, maintaining performance while saving inference costs.
limits: CoT vs direct only; no search or agent loops. Equals sign is a crude symbolic marker.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for a class-based S0 gate: the value of thinking depends on task class, and a cheap lexical cue captures most of it.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? (tools)
finding: Splitting plan from execution: CoT mostly helps execution of symbolic steps, but a symbolic solver beats CoT.
numbers: Paper reports CoT improves symbolic execution yet underperforms tool-augmented LLMs and plan-then-solver setups on math and logic tasks (abstract level; table numbers not recorded).
limits: Per-task numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: When a tool can do the computation, thinking tokens are worth less than a tool call. Gate should prefer tools over longer thought.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend huge compute on trivial questions, with extra solutions adding little accuracy.
numbers: For 'what is 2 plus 3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. 13 solutions on one trivial item. Most items give 2-4 solution rounds (76-80% of cases for QwQ-32B-Preview, 59-63% for R1). Self-training cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview at kept accuracy.
limits: Math sets (ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME). Two reasoning models. Efficiency metrics are the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Direct failure case for missing metareasoning: no stop rule once the first answer is correct. Supports a stop gate after first verified answer.

source: Chen et al. (2024) overthinking: first-correct analysis
finding: Most of the time the first solution is already right; later rounds add little and show low diversity.
numbers: Paper states overthinking patterns: contribute minimally to accuracy, lack diversity in strategies, occur more on simple problems. First-correctness share read from a figure as roughly 93-97% on ASDIV and MATH500 (approximate).
limits: Figure-read numbers are approximate.
agent_relevance: A stop rule 'verify once, then stop' captures most of the value on easy items.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Best way to spend test-time compute depends on question difficulty. A difficulty-adaptive allocation beats uniform best-of-N.
numbers: Compute-optimal strategy matches best-of-N using about 4x less test-time compute. FLOPs-matched: on easy and intermediate questions a smaller model plus test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model; on the hardest questions pretraining wins.
limits: PaLM 2-S* on MATH; difficulty from the model's own pass-rate bins. Predicting difficulty costs compute.
agent_relevance: Clearest AI result that VOC depends on difficulty. Gate needs a difficulty estimate; here the model's own pass rate worked.

source: Snell et al. (2024) (limits)
finding: On the hardest problems extra test-time compute gives little; easy questions favour sequential revision, harder ones favour parallel search.
numbers: Authors report the revision-vs-search split by difficulty and little benefit from test-time scaling on the most challenging questions (text-level, no single number).
limits: One model family, one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gate should have a give-up-or-escalate branch for hard items, not just think more.

source: Arora and Zanette (2025) Training language models to reason efficiently
finding: RL with a length penalty traces a compute-accuracy curve controlled by one coefficient. Savings are larger on easy problems.
numbers: 7B model: up to 50% fewer tokens with under 5% accuracy loss. By set: 16% fewer tokens on AIME24 (-3.3 points), 37% on MATH500 (-2.2), 65% on GSM8K (-1.7). Even alpha=0 shortens responses somewhat.
limits: Two open reasoning models (R1-Distill 1.5B and 7B). Accuracy does drop; hard sets lose more per token saved.
agent_relevance: Confirms the cost-benefit trade-off: easy tasks tolerate large cuts, hard ones little.

source: Damani et al. (2024) Learning how hard to think: input-adaptive allocation of LM computation
finding: A learned predictor of the reward distribution per input lets the system give more compute where it helps.
numbers: Code: same quality with up to 50% less compute; chat: up to 10% less. Routing: matches expensive decoder while calling it 50-75% of the time; value-augmentation routing saves 25-40% of expensive calls. Full test set gains modest (0-10% budget cut on some tasks), larger on tranches of extreme-variance queries (25-40%).
limits: About half the coding problems have zero success probability, so allocation can waste budget; the offline variant fixes this. Gains depend on spread of difficulty.
agent_relevance: If our task classes vary in difficulty a learned estimate pays; if uniform, gain is small. Need per-class pass-rate data.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1: controlling how long a reasoning model thinks with RL
finding: Training a model to follow a requested token budget gives smooth control of the compute-accuracy trade-off.
numbers: L1 (from R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) beats S1 budget forcing by up to 100% relative and 20% absolute at equal length; 20-25 points absolute at 512 and 1024 tokens; short-reasoning variants gain up to 10% at same length. L1-Exact about 1% below DeepScaleR-4K.
limits: Math benchmarks; 1.5B model; needs RL training.
agent_relevance: An explicit budget input works. A scaffold could pass a budget per state, but budget-following needs trained models.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute
finding: More reasoning can lower accuracy: negative value of computation is real.
numbers: Simple counting with distractors: Claude Opus 4 falls from near 100% to 85-90% as reasoning lengthens; DeepSeek R1 falls from 70% to 30% with five distractors in the natural-overthinking setup; o3 more stable. Five failure modes across four task families.
limits: Constructed tasks designed to break models; not typical workloads.
agent_relevance: Computation can have negative value. A gate needs a stop rule and distractor-resistant checks, not only a think-more option.

source: NoWait authors (2025) Wait, we don't need to Wait! Removing thinking tokens improves reasoning efficiency
finding: Suppressing self-reflection tokens such as Wait and Hmm shortens traces without hurting accuracy in R1-style models.
numbers: Chain-of-thought length cut 27-51% across five R1-style model series on ten text, image and video benchmarks, with utility kept (abstract and first page read).
limits: Training-free trick; effect on very hard problems not checked.
agent_relevance: Much reflection is low-value on average. Counter to forcing 'wait and double check' everywhere.

source: Callaway, Lieder et al. (2018) A resource-rational analysis of human planning
finding: Human planning clicks fit a VOC-optimal metareasoning model better than classic search heuristics.
numbers: Exp 1: 60 MTurk workers, 51 kept. Score 6.54 vs optimal 9.33 (about 70%). Table 1 raw likelihood scores: optimal 30625, best-first 31744, breadth-first 32387, depth-first 32454, directed cognition 34025, random 34579. Moves optimal given information 98.6%.
limits: Mouselab-MDP toy task with click cost; MTurk adults; small fixed tree.
agent_relevance: Humans are partly metarational; rival to single-heuristic accounts. Task-specific cost-benefit stop rules are plausible.

source: Callaway, Lieder et al. (2018) (deviations)
finding: People deviate from bounded optimality in systematic ways: they plan too little.
numbers: 45.0% of computations were sub-optimal but achieved 86.8% of the highest possible VOC (rationality quotient). Of deviations, 28.3% were stopping too early, 6.3% too late, 65.5% choosing the wrong node. Per-person rationality 0-98.5% of optimal VOC (mean 80.0%, SD 26.4%), maybe bimodal. First step inspected before second 72.6% vs 10.0%.
limits: Conference version; the 2022 journal version not read.
agent_relevance: Natural bias is to stop early. Check our agent for premature stops in logs.

source: Callaway, Lieder et al. (2018) Experiment 2
finding: The model discriminates between rival theories: people plan forward or backward depending on reward variance.
numbers: BIC optimal 21203 vs directed cognition 25354 vs best-first 29122 vs random 29313. Increasing-variance condition: first click on an end state 95.0% vs 0.3% in decreasing; score about 80.2% of optimal in both.
limits: Instructions told participants the reward structure.
agent_relevance: Strategy should adapt to where the uncertainty is, not follow a fixed order. Ties to choosing which sub-question to open first.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning, Nature Human Behaviour 6:1112
finding: Published version: best-first search near-optimal in some environments but not others; mouse-tracking fits the optimal model, not any single heuristic.
numbers: Abstract-level summary only, from a search result; no numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same as the 2018 lines.

source: Russell and Wefald (1991) Do the right thing / Principles of metareasoning
finding: Founding model: compute only while expected value of computation exceeds its time cost; practical systems use myopic one-step estimates.
numbers: From memory; not opened. The VOC equation was seen second-hand in De Sabbata et al. (read).
limits: Known limit: one-step VOC can be zero when several steps would pay.
agent_relevance: Defines the S0 gate and S6 trigger test. 'No gain from one more step' is not proof to stop.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, Behavioral and Brain Sciences
finding: Framework: derive heuristics as optimal use of limited computation; strategy selection as learned metareasoning.
numbers: From memory; not opened. Cited as a source in De Sabbata et al.
limits: Critics say cost terms are fitted post hoc.
agent_relevance: Cost terms are free parameters, so measure our own token cost per class rather than assume.

source: Sui et al. (2025) Stop overthinking: a survey on efficient reasoning for LLMs
finding: Survey organises efficiency methods (length penalties, adaptive budgets, early exit, routing) for reasoning models.
numbers: Only first sections skimmed; no table numbers recorded.
limits: Skim only; claims not checked.
agent_relevance: Pointer list for forward citations.

source: Synthesis: RaM vs length-penalty methods
finding: RaM paper cites concurrent long-to-short work (Arora and Zanette) with similar results; no head-to-head run exists in either paper.
numbers: Both cut tokens with accuracy roughly kept (RaM 23-42% fewer; Arora up to 50% at under 5% loss).
limits: Different bases (pretrained vs reasoning models).
agent_relevance: The VOC framing may add little over a plain length penalty. A threshold gate may be enough.

source: Synthesis: Arora and Zanette, Chen et al., Snell et al.
finding: Independent methods agree: token savings are largest where problems are easy.
numbers: GSM8K -65% tokens (-1.7 pts) vs AIME24 -16% (-3.3 pts) in Arora; Chen finds overthinking more common on simple problems; Snell finds easy items gain most from sequential revision.
limits: Different models and methods; synthesis, not a single test.
agent_relevance: Supports a class-dependent gate: strong cut on easy classes, keep budget on hard ones.

source: Snell et al. (2024) (difficulty estimate)
finding: Difficulty is estimated from the base model's own pass rate (5 bins); strategy is then chosen per bin.
numbers: Two-fold cross validation on each difficulty bin selects the best hyperparameters; the paper treats difficulty as a sufficient statistic for choosing the strategy.
limits: Estimating difficulty costs samples that count against the budget.
agent_relevance: Our S0 gate can use class pass-rate history as the difficulty estimate; stable estimates need enough prior runs per class.

source: Gema et al. (2025) (rival failure mode: Claude vs o-series)
finding: Models fail differently with longer thought: Claude gets distracted, o-series overfit problem framing, others drift to spurious features.
numbers: Abstract lists five modes; in counting-with-distractors o3 stays stable in the controlled setup but shows a weak decline in the natural setup.
limits: Model-specific; may change with versions.
agent_relevance: Stop rules should be tested per model, since the cost of extra thought is not the same across models.
